Prompt-level intervention (schema-informed prompting) reduces violations by ~62% but cannot eliminate them — certain relation types retain 25-30% violation rates even with explicit constraint descriptions. OntoCoDec provides **near-complete elimination (DR 15.4%→0.93%, ↓94%) at zero or positive F1 impact** through automatic ontology-to-decoder constraint compilation with two complementary layers.\\n\\n**Phase 2 confirmed (D012 bootstrap CI, v2 fix)**: Grammar+Semantic dual-layer constrained decoding reduces domain/range violations by 94%, eliminates entity-type and relation-vocabulary violations entirely (→0%). F1 impact is **dataset-dependent**:\\n- SciERC: Rel F1 neutral (+0.13pp, p=0.58), Ent F1 neutral (-0.03pp, p=0.53)\\n- DocRED: Rel F1 **significantly improved** (+0.50pp, p<0.001, 95% CI [+0.23, +0.81]); Ent F1 **significantly improved** (+1.23pp, p<0.001, 95% CI [+0.94, +1.55])\\n- Mechanism: grammar 消除 OOV relation names (DocRED RV 29.66%→0.03%) + 非标 entity types (ET 2.48%→0%)。all_set F1 方法下 OOV=FP → fewer FP → higher precision/F1。SciERC baseline RV/ET 已很低，效果不显著。\\n- **Grammar 层是 F1 提升的唯一来源**: grammar_only Ent F1=59.38% ≈ full_s1 59.37% (Δ+0.01pp, p=0.66)。Semantic 层对 F1 无额外贡献，专注 DR reduction。\\n\\n## Core Claims\\n\\n### Claim 1 (Empirical): Violation Landscape\\nLLM-based IE systems violate ontology type constraints at non-trivial rates (15.4% per-triple on SciERC, 18.7% on DocRED). Violations are **not uniformly distributed** — they concentrate on relation types with tight domain/range constraints (Feature-of 33.5%, Compare 42.4%) while loose-constraint relations show near-zero violation (Used-for 0.8%).\\n\\n**Key insight**: Violation rate is driven by **constraint tightness**, not ontology size. A small ontology with tight constraints can produce more violations than a large ontology with loose constraints.\\n\\n**D014 修订**: DR reduction ceiling 由 **tightness × model RV baseline** 共同决定，非 tightness 单因素。Llama DocRED DR↓90.2% vs Qwen DR↓44.7%（同一 ontology τ̄=0.842）。机制：Qwen RV=29.66% >> Llama RV=16.03% → grammar 层将 OOV triples 强制匹配有效关系名 → 揭露大量 latent DR violations → 残余 DR 更高。这是比单一 tightness 更深的 insight。\\n\\n**Evidence**: SciERC (7 relations) 15.4%; DocRED (96 relations) 18.7% — comparable rates despite 14× ontology size difference. Schema-informed prompt on DocRED only achieves DR↓32% (vs SciERC ↓62%), confirming **prompt-level intervention scales poorly with ontology complexity**.\\n\\n### Claim 2 (Empirical): Prompt Insufficiency\\nSchema-informed prompting (explicitly describing domain/range constraints in the prompt) reduces but does not eliminate violations:\\n- Overall: 15.4% → 5.78% (-62.4%), still above 5%\\n- Per-relation: Compare 42.4% → 27.6%, Evaluate-for 24.1% → 29.9% (**worse**)\\n- Prompt intervention is unreliable at the per-relation level — some relations improve, one regresses\\n\\n**Narrative**: This is NOT about \\\"5.78% barely above 5%\\\". The story is: **prompt-level intervention is fundamentally unreliable as a guarantee mechanism**. It works statistically but cannot provide per-instance compliance. Three specific relation types retain >10% violation rates with schema-informed prompts. For safety-critical IE (biomedical, legal, regulatory), statistical reduction is insufficient — guaranteed compliance is required.\\n\\n### Claim 3 (Methodological): Composable Constraint Framework\\nOntoCoDec automatically compiles IE ontology schemas into two composable constraint layers:\\n1. **Grammar layer** (XGrammar): JSON structure + type vocabulary constraints (CFG-expressible)\\n2. **Semantic layer** (TypeConstraintProcessor): Cross-field domain/range constraints via stateful entity registry + dynamic logit masking\\n\\nThe two layers are **complementary with enabling dependency**: grammar ensures every generated relation type is in the valid vocabulary, which enables the semantic layer to look up and enforce domain/range rules for that type. Without grammar, the semantic layer encounters unknown relation types and cannot enforce constraints (explaining why semantic_only achieves only ↓24% vs full_s1 ↓94%). This is NOT \\\"synergistic\\\" (mutual amplification) — grammar is a prerequisite for semantic, not vice versa.\\n\\nThe two layers compose via bitwise AND of token masks. Recommended framing: \\\"Grammar and semantic constraints compose via bitwise AND with an enabling dependency: grammar ensures structural validity, enabling semantic constraints to enforce domain/range rules. When constraint tightness creates empty intersection between layers, the system degrades gracefully to grammar-only constraints, maintaining structural validity as a guaranteed floor.\\\"\\n\\n**Graceful degradation + Fallback 频率量化** (D008 + Reviewer 发现):\\nWhen $M_{semantic} \\\\cap M_{grammar} = \\\\emptyset$, the system falls back to grammar-only control.\\n\\n**关键量化数据（Reviewer 从日志挖掘）**:\\n- Llama DocRED full_s1: **32,921 次 fallback / 577 docs = ~57 次/doc**\\n- Llama SciERC full_s1: **5,882 次 fallback / 550 docs = ~10.7 次/doc**\\n- DocRED fallback 频率是 SciERC 的 **5.3×**\\n- Qwen DocRED fallback 率未知（日志当时无 fallback logging，需估算）\\n\\n**这直接解释了 DocRED DR 残余 10.19% vs SciERC 0.93%**: 更多 token 位置退化为 grammar-only → grammar-only 的 DR 已知为 26.17% → 高 fallback = 高残余 DR。\\n\\n**论文建议**: 在 §5 tightness 段报告 fallback 率，定义 \\\"Constraint Coverage\\\" 指标（semantic masking 实际生效的 token 比例）。这把 \\\"10.19% DR 残余\\\" 从弱点变成可量化分析的 finding。Frame as \\\"engineering robustness\\\" in §4; fallback 频率 + tightness 作为 §5 定量分析。\\n\\n**Decidability taxonomy**: Constraints classified by prefix-decidability:\\n- (a) Purely local: entity type ∈ vocabulary (grammar layer)\\n- (b) Prefix-decidable with state: relation argument types compatible with domain/range (semantic layer, requires entity registry)\\n- (c) Truly non-local: forward coreference — out of scope for forward-only decoding\\n\\n### Claim 4 (Methodological): S1 vs S2 Decoding Strategies — Architectural Ablation\\n- S1 (single-pass): Both layers applied throughout generation. **Recommended primary strategy** — simpler, slightly better metrics across the board.\\n- S2 (two-pass): Pass 1 extracts entities (grammar-only), Pass 2 generates relations with input-dependent grammar compiled from Pass 1 entities.\\n\\n**S2 full results (551/551 SciERC)**: DR 0.97% (vs S1 0.93%), CF 8.03% (vs S1 9.9%), R-F1 8.03% (vs S1 8.36%). S2 does NOT solve CF — the 1.87pp reduction is not significant. S2 also slightly worse on DR and F1. **S2 is an architectural variant demonstrating framework flexibility, not a CF solution.** Position in paper as ablation (Section 5 or Appendix), not as a core contribution.\\n\\n⚠️ **Do NOT cite pilot50 DR=0% as S2 evidence** — small-sample artifact; full run shows DR=0.97%. Per-relation S2 DR is worse than S1 on Compare (4.6% vs 2.82%), Part-of (1.25% vs 0%), Used-for (0.12% vs 0%).\\n\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns\\n\\n### C1: \\\"5.78% is barely above 5% — threshold is arbitrary\\\"\\n**Response**: Don't argue about the threshold. Argue about per-relation distribution: Compare (27.6%), Evaluate-for (29.9%), Feature-of (11.3%) have double-digit violation rates with schema-informed prompt. The value proposition is per-relation guaranteed compliance, not overall statistical rate.\\n\\n### C2: \\\"Why not just post-hoc filter?\\\"\\n**Response (D013, 实验结果已出)**:\\n\\nPost-hoc filtering 实验结果：post-hoc F1 > OntoCoDec F1（SciERC 8.63 vs 8.36, DocRED 9.61 vs 8.24）——因 low F1 regime 下移除 FP 大幅提升 precision。\\n\\n**论文 framing（不以 F1 论高低，多维对比）**:\\n1. **Recall 维度（核心论点）**: OntoCoDec recall 上升 (SciERC +0.20pp, DocRED +0.56pp) = 概率质量重分配到合法 token 生效。Post-hoc recall 下降 (SciERC -0.72pp, DocRED -1.06pp) = 正确 triple 被误删。\\n2. **Information coverage**: DocRED post-hoc 丢弃 **48.1%** triples（近半数信息丢失），SciERC 16.8%。OntoCoDec 保留全部 triple slots。\\n3. **Operational**: OntoCoDec 产出即合规、无需后处理、支持流式。Post-hoc 需额外管线、不适用实时场景。\\n4. **Precision trade-off（诚实承认）**: \\\"Post-hoc achieves higher precision by removing a large fraction of triples, many of which are incorrect. This trades information coverage for precision — valid when FP are costly, but inadequate when completeness matters.\\\"\\n\\n数据表：SciERC post-hoc rejection 16.8%, OntoCoDec recall 11.60 vs post-hoc 10.68; DocRED post-hoc rejection 48.1%, OntoCoDec recall 10.02 vs post-hoc 8.40。\\n\\n**Reviewer 补充发现（D013 后）**:\\n5. **ET 残余**：post-hoc 只删 triples 不改 entity list，残余 ET=0.4% (SciERC) / 2.47% (DocRED)。OntoCoDec ET=0%。Post-hoc 无法解决 entity type 违规。\\n6. **127 个被删 TP (DocRED)**：过滤前 TP=1137，过滤后 TP=1010。丢失的 127 个 TP（11.2%）是正确提取但 entity type 违规的 triple。OntoCoDec 通过生成时强制合法 type 保留这些 TP——\\\"prevent vs detect\\\" 核心论据的具体数据。\\n7. **OntoCoDec+post-hoc 组合**（future work idea）：先 constrain 再 filter 残余 DR。低优先级，May 19 前不做。\\n\\n### C3: \\\"Bitwise AND of two masks is not novel\\\"\\n**Response**: The novelty is not the AND operation — it's (a) the automatic compilation from ontology definitions (zero-code schema compliance), (b) the stateful entity registry enabling cross-field constraints during autoregressive generation, (c) the decidability taxonomy providing theoretical guidance, and (d) the systematic violation landscape measurement motivating the approach.\\n\\n### C4: \\\"Evaluate-for violation rate increases with schema-informed prompt\\\"\\n**Response (prior-constraint conflict framework)**: Evaluate-for has 23/36 valid pairs; Method→Task is invalid for Evaluate-for but natural in the LLM's distributional prior (\\\"Method X evaluates for Task Y\\\" is semantically plausible). ## Target Venue

## Title

(D015: "Near-Complete" dropped — DocRED residual DR=10.21% (Qwen) 不算 near-complete。论文贡献是方法，不是特定消除率。SciERC 0.93% 和 DocRED 2.55% (Llama) 可在正文中描述为 near-complete，但 title 不宜 overclaim。)

LLM-based IE systems produce systematic ontology constraint violations concentrated in specific relation types. ## Core Claims

### Claim 1 (Empirical): Violation Landscape
LLM-based IE systems violate ontology type constraints at non-trivial rates (15.4% per-triple on SciERC, 18.7% on DocRED). Violations are **not uniformly distributed** — they concentrate on relation types with tight domain/range constraints (Feature-of 33.5%, Compare 42.4%) while loose-constraint relations show near-zero violation (Used-for 0.8%).

Schema-informed prompting (explicitly describing domain/range constraints in the prompt) reduces but does not eliminate violations:
- Overall: 15.4% → 5.78% (-62.4%), still above 5%
- Per-relation: Compare 42.4% → 27.6%, Evaluate-for 24.1% → 29.9% (**worse**)

**Narrative**: This is NOT about "5.78% barely above 5%". The story is: **prompt-level intervention is fundamentally unreliable as a guarantee mechanism**. It works statistically but cannot provide per-instance compliance. Three specific relation types retain >10% violation rates with schema-informed prompts. For safety-critical IE (biomedical, legal, regulatory), statistical reduction is insufficient — guaranteed compliance is required.

### Claim 3 (Methodological): Composable Constraint Framework
OntoCoDec automatically compiles IE ontology schemas into two composable constraint layers:
1. **Grammar layer** (XGrammar): JSON structure + type vocabulary constraints (CFG-expressible)
2. **Semantic layer** (TypeConstraintProcessor): Cross-field domain/range constraints via stateful entity registry + dynamic logit masking

The two layers are **complementary with enabling dependency**: grammar ensures every generated relation type is in the valid vocabulary, which enables the semantic layer to look up and enforce domain/range rules for that type. def normalize_type(t, valid_types, type_map=None):
    """Case-insensitive type matching with common aliases."""

OK, I now have the ontology constraints. Let me understand the DR violation structure:

For each relation type, there are specific valid (head_type, tail_type) pairs. A DR violation occurs when a triple uses a valid relation type but with an invalid (head_type, tail_type) pair.

Key observations from the constraints:
- **Used-for**: 35 valid pairs — very loose constraint, almost all type pairs are valid → low DR expected
- **Feature-of**: Truncated but likely more restrictive
- **Evaluate-for**: 23 valid pairs — moderately restrictive


- **Compare, Conjunction**: Likely more restrictive

Looking at the W5 output samples, I see a couple of valid triples: "photometric calibration" and "scanning method" both typed as Method with Used-for between them, and "subpixel precision" as Metric with "method" as Generic in an Evaluate-for relation. These match the valid pairs, but the sample size is too small to draw conclusions about violation rates.

Now I'm thinking about what happens when we apply LoRA fine-tuning to SciERC data. The zero-shot baseline had 18.46% DR, and the key question is whether training on the correct entity and relation types from the ontology significantly reduces this. If the model truly internalizes the constraints, we'd expect DR to drop substantially—but if it just learns the output format without understanding the underlying rules, DR could stay elevated. The tight-constraint relations like Feature-of and Compare were the main sources of errors before, so whether LoRA brings DR below 2% will tell us a lot about whether the model actually learned composable constraints or just memorized patterns.

Given the training set size of 1762 samples, I'd expect the model to pick up common type pair distributions, though rarer combinations might still cause violations. My intuition is DR probably lands somewhere in the 3-8% range after fine-tuning, but I need to see the actual results to know for sure.

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.

- review: Review a pull request

But there's a timing issue here: D020 was issued at 14:59 UTC on 2026-05-15, while w1_cf_fallback_docred was submitted at 15:03 UTC the same day. The Agent actually submitted this experiment 4 minutes after the cancellation directive, which means it shouldn't have been started. D020's reasoning mentions that the mechanism is already well-explained at the theoretical level, so there's no need for cross-model or cross-dataset validation.

Yet the Agent went ahead and submitted w1_cf_fallback_docred anyway — a Qwen3-8B run on DocRED that directly contradicts this assessment. Looking at the timestamps more carefully, the job was created in PREPARING state at 10:32:53 UTC but didn't submit until 15:03:45 UTC, a gap of over 4 hours. The tight 4-minute window between D020 and submission suggests the job might have already been queued and auto-submitted before the cancellation was processed, though it's also possible the Agent deliberately proceeded despite the decision or there's a code reversion issue at play.

The practical reality is that w1_cf_fallback_docred loaded the CF-modified code before the 15:22 revert and is running it in memory, so it's actually testing what it's supposed to test. While this does consume GPU resources on cuda:1 for 5-6 hours, it doesn't interfere with the W5 critical path on cuda:0, so the impact is manageable. I should flag this as a discrepancy but keep it at an informational level rather than treating it as a blocker.

I'm noticing a few documentation issues that need attention: the ROADMAP GPU section is outdated with stale PIDs, experiment_plan.yaml is empty with no formal tracking, and there's a minor timing discrepancy with w1_cf_fallback_docred being submitted after the D020 cancellation. content.content:
1	# W1 CF-Fallback SciERC Pilot — Detailed Analysis
2	
3	**Experiment**: `w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot`  vs  baseline `phase2_scierc_full_s1` (Qwen, SciERC test, 551 samples, full S1 stage)
4	**Status**: DONE / negative (DR escalates while CF is nearly eliminated)
5	**Date**: 2026-05-15
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. Executive Summary
10	
11	The CF-priority fallback policy in W1 was designed to eliminate cross-field-consistency (CF) violations by preferring previously-registered entity types over fresh domain/range masks. The pilot confirms CF is nearly eradicated (9.90 % → **0.04 %**, a 244-of-245 reduction), but at a severe cost: per-triple domain-range (DR) violation rate explodes from **0.93 % → 14.78 %** (+13.85 pp, ×15.9). Of 17 024 semantic-mask invocations, only **58.9 % (10 024)** were "effective" — the remaining **36.6 % (6 237)** were silently overridden by the grammar-first guard (semantic ∩ grammar = ∅) and another **4.5 % (763)** by the CF registry. R-F1 / E-F1 are statistically unchanged (8.36 → 8.23, 30.98 → 30.98), so the move is a pure DR-vs-CF trade with no quality win.
12

**Experiment**: `w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot`  vs  baseline `phase2_scierc_full_s1` (Qwen, SciERC test, 551 samples, full S1 stage)
**Status**: DONE / negative (DR escalates while CF is nearly eliminated)
**Date**: 2026-05-15

---

## 1. Executive Summary

The CF-priority fallback policy in W1 was designed to eliminate cross-field-consistency (CF) violations by preferring previously-registered entity types over fresh domain/range masks. The pilot confirms CF is nearly eradicated (9.90 % → **0.04 %**, a 244-of-245 reduction), but at a severe cost: per-triple domain-range (DR) violation rate explodes from **0.93 % → 14.78 %** (+13.85 pp, ×15.9). Of 17 024 semantic-mask invocations, only **58.9 % (10 024)** were "effective" — the remaining **36.6 % (6 237)** were silently overridden by the grammar-first guard (semantic ∩ grammar = ∅) and another **4.5 % (763)** by the CF registry. R-F1 / E-F1 are statistically unchanged (8.36 → 8.23, 30.98 → 30.98), so the move is a pure DR-vs-CF trade with no quality win.

The most striking result: **the pilot's DR rate (14.78 %) recovers 96.2 % of the fully unconstrained DR rate (15.37 %)**. | Grammar-first override | 6 237 | 0 (mathematically possible if every override happened to pick a valid-pair token by chance) | 239 (if every new DR violation came from this channel) |
| CF-registry override | 763 | 0 | 239 |
| "Effective" semantic mask path | 10 024 | 16 (baseline residual; mask is enforced on this branch) | 16 |

The strict lower bound on the "effective" channel = baseline DR (16) — semantic masking actively enforced on those 10 024 steps still left 16 violations because the per-step token-level mask cannot prevent every multi-step type-pair combination once the head_type is committed (intra-triple coupling). All other DR escalation must come from the two override channels.

### 5.2 Why grammar-first dominates — the "return to unconstrained" phenomenon

The grammar-first guard activates when the **per-relation domain/range constraint at the current token position would leave the grammar-valid token set empty**. Concretely, this happens when:
1. The model has already committed `relation=R, head_type=H` (or it is about to emit `tail_type` in a tight relation), **and**
2. No valid `tail_type` token under `valid_pairs(R, H, *)` is also currently grammar-valid (e.g., next-token must start with `O` for `OtherScientificTerm` because of grammar prefix state, but `OtherScientificTerm` isn't in `range(R, H)`).

For a relation like Compare with only 17/36 valid pairs, the probability that a randomly-arrived-at head_type leaves a non-empty tail_type intersection is structurally low — hence Compare's 39.4 % pilot DR.

**Critical finding: the pilot DR rate (14.78 %) is 96.2 % of the fully unconstrained rate (15.37 %).** The per-relation recovery rates (see §2) confirm this is not a coincidence — for every relation with tightness > 0.25, the pilot's DR exceeds 93 % of the unconstrained level. The grammar-first fallback does not add a small number of new violations; it *restores* the system to its pre-constraint behavior. The 3.8 % residual gap (15.37 − 14.78 = 0.59 pp) corresponds almost entirely to Used-for, the loosest relation, where semantic masking still operates on the majority of mask calls.

Verification of channel attribution requires the per-mask-call relation-tagged log (see §3); we recommend adding it before W3 (Llama × SciERC, Llama × DocRED) runs so the same analysis on Llama is directly attributable.

### 5.3 Per-relation new DR violation type-pair signatures

(From JSONL re-analysis; full table in Section 2.) Three patterns repeat across relations:

- **OST-as-bucket**: 67 new violations name `OtherScientificTerm` on at least one side of an invalid pair across Feature-of / Compare / Part-of / Hyponym-of. The model uses OST as a low-specificity fallback type; the CF registry consequently locks it in across calls.
- **Task ↔ OST**: 60 new violations (Hyponym-of, Feature-of, Compare, Part-of). Tasks frequently co-occur with phrases the model parses as OST rather than re-using the Task tag.
- **Generic explosion in Feature-of**: 33 new (Generic, Generic) Feature-of violations. Feature-of does *not* allow (Generic, Generic) in the SciERC training-derived constraint, but Generic is by far the most common fallback type the model emits.

---

## 6. Paper Implications (Reviewer Framing)

The Reviewer's suggestion was to make the **attempted vs effective** decomposition explicit in the paper. This pilot directly supports four load-bearing claims for the methods section:

1. **Mask-invocation count is not enforcement strength.** On Qwen-SciERC, only 58.9 % of semantic-mask calls were effective; 36.6 % were silently overridden by the grammar-first guard and 4.5 % by the CF registry. Papers that report "constrained decoding was applied at 100 % of decoding steps" without this decomposition systematically overstate the contribution of semantic constraints.

2. **CF and DR live in a single violation budget.** Baseline violation budget (DR + CF) = 10.83 %. Pilot budget = 14.82 % (DR 14.78 + CF 0.04). Eliminating CF cost +3.99 pp of total violations — the constraint did not vanish, it moved. This is a clean negative result motivating a *joint* CF + DR scheduler instead of a hierarchical fallback.

3. **Hierarchical fallback ≈ no constraint at all.** The pilot's DR rate (14.78 %) recovers 96.2 % of the unconstrained DR rate (15.37 %). Per-relation, the recovery exceeds 93 % for every relation with tightness > 0.25. This is not a partial degradation — the grammar-first fallback mechanism effectively *disables* semantic enforcement whenever a schema has non-trivial constraints. The only relation where enforcement survives is Used-for (tightness = 0.03), which is loose enough that semantic ∩ grammar is almost never empty.

4. **Tightness predicts fallback risk.** Across relations the per-relation ΔDR rank-correlates with tightness (Compare ≫ Part-of ≈ Hyponym-of ≈ Feature-of ≫ Used-for). Spearman ρ = 0.50 (n = 7), Pearson r = 0.67 (p = 0.098). Schemas with high-tightness relations need an alternative enforcement strategy (joint product mask, beam-search with backtracking, or training-time alignment) — fallback-style decoding cannot maintain DR on tight schemas without a quality penalty.

The downstream F1 numbers (R-F1 ±0.13, E-F1 ±0.00) confirm that the move is policy-neutral for end-task accuracy. The *paper-level* contribution of W1 is therefore the negative finding plus the decomposition — both of which strengthen, rather than weaken, the framing of OntoCoDec's joint-mask design as the principled alternative.
